claims.text: Thermal processing route, specifically heating and cooling rates, governs formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
A slower, controlled thermal ramp promotes single-phase solid-solution formation relative to rapid thermal cycling.
An intermediate high-temperature dwell facilitates uniform atomic interdiffusion.
Slower thermal processing and an intermediate dwell facilitate homogeneous nucleation.
The proposed intervention is slower heating, an isothermal high-temperature hold, and slower cooling compared with the rapid-cycle baseline.
Rapid heating and cooling typically lead to metastable phases and elemental segregation in the stated compositional regime.
A prolonged dwell enhances atomic diffusion and nanoscale compositional homogenization.
Enhanced diffusion and homogenization enable controlled nucleation of a single-phase structure.
Slowing the thermal cycle gives atoms sufficient time to overcome kinetic barriers.
Overcoming kinetic barriers allows atoms to arrange into a thermodynamically more stable, homogeneous solid solution.
Rapid temperature changes induce phase separation or elemental segregation.
Slower thermal cycling ensures more controlled particle morphology.
Slower thermal cycling reduces the risk of high thermal decomposition.
Controlled thermal processing will produce a more homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution structure than rapid processing.
Controlled thermal processing will improve control over nanoparticle morphology.
The predicted structure will exhibit uniform elemental distribution and stable crystallographic order.
The rapid-processing baseline frequently exhibits phase separation, elemental clustering, structural defects, and morphological irregularities.
The hypothesis is limited to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements under kinetically trapping thermal regimes.
The intervention's effects may differ when the alloying elements change or diffusion is not rate limiting.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in single-phase formation, segregation, or morphology relative to the rapid-cycle control would falsify the hypothesis.
